title: What is the difference between Event Notification (a minimal event carrying just an id + event name + a link to fetch details) and Event-Carried State Transfer (the event carries the data consumers need), what is the "fat event / god event" anti-pattern (broadcasting the whole aggregate "just in case"), and how do you decide between the two (coupling vs extra calls, with versioned schemas either way)?
shortTitle: Event Notification versus Event-Carried State Transfer

s1_definition.profdef: Event Notification is a style where the event is minimal — an event ID, the event name, the aggregate ID, and usually a link — and the consumer must call back to the producer to fetch the details it needs, keeping payloads tiny but adding a synchronous callback and runtime coupling. Event-Carried State Transfer puts the data the consumer needs directly inside the event, so consumers can act without calling back, improving autonomy and read availability at the cost of larger payloads and some data duplication. The fat event or god event anti-pattern is broadcasting the entire aggregate state just in case, which leaks internals, bloats the topic, and couples every consumer to the producer's full model; you decide between the two styles by trading coupling and callback load against payload size and duplication, always using a deliberately versioned schema either way.
s1_definition.analogy: When a transfer completes at National Bank of India, the transfer department can tell the SMS department in two ways. Event Notification is a short memo: "Transfer T-123 happened for account SAV2001 — call us if you need details." The SMS department then phones back to get the amount and beneficiary. Event-Carried State Transfer is a fuller memo: "Transfer T-123 happened: Rs.50000 to BENEF-77 from SAV2001" — now the SMS department can act immediately without phoning back. The fat-event anti-pattern is photocopying the transfer department's entire internal file — every private note, risk score, and scratch calculation — and mailing it to everyone just in case, which is wasteful and exposes secrets nobody should see.
s1_definition.oneliner: Event Notification sends a tiny pointer and makes consumers call back; Event-Carried State Transfer sends the data consumers need so they act independently; never send the whole aggregate just in case.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Event Notification is a style where the event is minimal — an event ID, the event name, the aggregate ID, and usually a link — and the consumer must call back to the producer to fetch the details it needs, keeping payloads tiny but adding a synchronous callback and runtime coupling. Event-Carried State Transfer puts the data the consumer needs directly inside the event, so consumers can act without calling back, improving autonomy and read availability at the cost of larger payloads and some data duplication. The fat event or god event anti-pattern is broadcasting the entire aggregate state just in case, which leaks internals, bloats the topic, and couples every consumer to the producer's full model; you decide between the two styles by trading coupling and callback load against payload size and duplication, always using a deliberately versioned schema either way.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** When a transfer completes at National Bank of India, the transfer department can tell the SMS department in two ways. Event Notification is a short memo: "Transfer T-123 happened for account SAV2001 — call us if you need details." The SMS department then phones back to get the amount and beneficiary. Event-Carried State Transfer is a fuller memo: "Transfer T-123 happened: Rs.50000 to BENEF-77 from SAV2001" — now the SMS department can act immediately without phoning back. The fat-event anti-pattern is photocopying the transfer department's entire internal file — every private note, risk score, and scratch calculation — and mailing it to everyone just in case, which is wasteful and exposes secrets nobody should see.

**One line to remember:** Event Notification sends a tiny pointer and makes consumers call back; Event-Carried State Transfer sends the data consumers need so they act independently; never send the whole aggregate just in case.

sections.s2_technical:
Event Notification keeps the event as small as possible. The payload is essentially an announcement: event ID, event type, the aggregate ID that changed, a timestamp, and often a link or enough identity for the consumer to fetch the current state from the producer's API. The consumer reacts by calling back to get exactly the fields it needs at the moment it needs them. The benefits are small payloads, no stale data in the event (the consumer always fetches fresh state), and the producer exposes little in the event itself. The costs are a synchronous callback per event, which reintroduces runtime coupling and a dependency on the producer's availability — if the producer is down, consumers that need details are stuck — and extra load on the producer's API, which can be significant at high event volumes.

Event-Carried State Transfer puts the data the consumer needs inside the event. When a transfer completes, the event carries the amount, the beneficiary, and the account, so the notification service can send the SMS with no callback at all. The benefits are consumer autonomy and resilience: consumers can act even if the producer is temporarily down, there is no callback load, and consumers can maintain their own local read models fed purely by events. The costs are larger payloads, some data duplication across services, and the possibility that the data in the event is a snapshot at emission time that could be slightly stale by the time it is consumed, which you must reason about.

The fat event or god event anti-pattern is the failure mode of over-applying state transfer. Instead of carrying just the fields consumers actually need, the producer serializes the entire aggregate — every field, including internal-only ones — and broadcasts it just in case some consumer might want something. This is bad for several reasons: it leaks the producer's internal model, turning the event into a de facto exposure of private structure; it bloats the topic and network; it tightly couples every consumer to the full model so any internal change risks breaking them; and it obscures the real contract because nobody knows which fields are actually part of the agreement. The fix is to design the event around the meaningful domain fact and include only the fields that genuine consumers need, treating the event schema as a curated contract rather than a database dump.

Deciding between the two styles is a trade-off. Favor Event-Carried State Transfer when consumer autonomy and resilience matter, when callback load would be heavy, or when consumers maintain local read models — which is common and often the better default in event-driven architectures. Favor Event Notification when the detail data is large or sensitive, when freshness is critical so a stale snapshot is unacceptable, or when few consumers need the details so the callback cost is low. A pragmatic hybrid is to carry the commonly-needed fields in the event and include a link for consumers that occasionally need the fuller, current state. Regardless of style, the schema must be deliberately versioned using something like Avro or Protobuf with a Schema Registry, because both styles create a contract that consumers depend on, and both must evolve without breaking them.

A senior engineer adds that the choice interacts with coupling direction. Event Notification couples consumers to the producer at runtime (they must call it); Event-Carried State Transfer couples them to the producer's schema at design time (they parse its fields). You are always choosing which coupling you prefer, and you minimize both by keeping events lean, versioned, and focused on the domain fact.
sections.s3_banking:
The real problem: National Bank of India's transfer service emits an event when a transfer completes, and the notification service must send an SMS. We examine both event styles and the fat-event anti-pattern.

Problem 1 — With Event Notification, the transfer service emits only "TransferCompleted, id T-123, account SAV2001." The notification service must call the transfer service's API to fetch the amount and beneficiary before it can send the SMS. If the transfer service is down, the SMS cannot be sent. This shows the callback cost and runtime coupling.

Problem 2 — With Event-Carried State Transfer, the event carries the amount and beneficiary, so the notification service sends the SMS immediately, even if the transfer service is temporarily down. This shows consumer autonomy, at the cost of a slightly bigger payload.

Problem 3 — The fat-event anti-pattern would serialize the entire internal transfer aggregate — internal ledger reference, risk bucket, internal flags — into the event. This leaks internals and couples consumers to fields they must not depend on. We show why it is wrong and how the curated state-transfer event avoids it.

What the code will do: a runnable demo emits all three event shapes for the same transfer. `NotificationViaNotification` consumes a minimal notification event and must call back a `TransferApi` to get details (and fails gracefully when the API is down). `NotificationViaStateTransfer` consumes a curated state-transfer event and acts with no callback. A `FatEventDemo` shows the bloated god event and logs a warning about leaked internals, contrasted with the slim curated event.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a completed transfer T-123 for Rs.50000 on account SAV2001 to beneficiary BENEF-77.

Step 1 (notification): The producer emits a minimal notification event carrying only the event ID, type, transfer ID, account ID, and a details link. The payload is tiny.

Step 2 (notification): The notification consumer receives it and must call the transfer API to fetch the amount and beneficiary. With the producer up, it gets the details and sends the SMS. This callback is the runtime coupling.

Step 3 (notification): We mark the producer as down and deliver the same event again. The callback returns nothing, so the consumer cannot send the SMS and logs a severe block. This demonstrates the availability dependency of Event Notification.

Step 4 (state transfer): The producer emits a curated state-transfer event carrying the amount and beneficiary directly. The payload is larger but self-sufficient.

Step 5 (state transfer): The notification consumer sends the SMS immediately with no callback, so it works even when the producer is down. This demonstrates consumer autonomy and resilience.

Step 6 (fat event): The producer emits a god event that also includes the internal ledger reference and risk bucket. The demo logs a severe warning that this leaks internals and couples consumers to the producer's private model, which is the anti-pattern to avoid.

Final output:

```
15:00:00 INFO    ===== EVENT NOTIFICATION (minimal; consumer calls back) =====
15:00:00 INFO    [NOTIFY-N] fetched details, SMS: Rs.50000 to BENEF-77
15:00:00 SEVERE  [NOTIFY-N] producer DOWN — cannot fetch details for T-123 → SMS blocked
15:00:00 INFO    ===== EVENT-CARRIED STATE TRANSFER (data in event; no callback) =====
15:00:00 INFO    [NOTIFY-S] SMS immediately (no callback): Rs.50000 to BENEF-77
15:00:00 INFO    ===== FAT / GOD EVENT (anti-pattern) =====
15:00:00 SEVERE  [FAT] god event leaks internals: internalRef=LEDGER-ab12 riskBucket=2 — couples consumers to producer internals (AVOID)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Event Notification and Event-Carried State Transfer are two ways to shape an event, and the difference is what the event carries and therefore what the consumer must do. Event Notification keeps the event tiny — an event ID, the event name, the aggregate ID that changed, and usually a link — and the consumer calls back to the producer to fetch whatever details it needs. The upside is small payloads and always-fresh data because the consumer fetches current state, but the downside is a synchronous callback per event, which reintroduces runtime coupling and a dependency on the producer being up, plus extra load on the producer's API at scale. Event-Carried State Transfer puts the data the consumer needs inside the event, so the consumer can act with no callback at all. The upside is consumer autonomy and resilience — it works even if the producer is temporarily down, there is no callback load, and consumers can build their own local read models from events — while the downside is larger payloads, some duplication, and a snapshot that may be slightly stale by consumption time.

The fat event or god event is what happens when you over-apply state transfer and simply serialize the entire aggregate, every field including internal-only ones, and broadcast it just in case. That is an anti-pattern because it leaks the producer's internal model, bloats the topic, couples every consumer to the full structure so any internal change can break them, and obscures what the real contract even is. The fix is to design the event around the meaningful domain fact and include only the fields genuine consumers actually need, treating the schema as a curated contract rather than a database dump.

Deciding between the two is a trade-off I reason about explicitly. I favor state transfer when consumer autonomy and resilience matter, when callback load would be heavy, or when consumers maintain local read models, and in event-driven systems that is often the better default. I favor notification when the detail data is large or sensitive, when freshness is so critical that a stale snapshot is unacceptable, or when so few consumers need the details that the callback cost is negligible. A pragmatic hybrid carries the commonly needed fields and includes a link for the rare consumer that needs the fuller current state. Either way the schema must be deliberately versioned with Avro or Protobuf and a Schema Registry, because both styles create a contract consumers depend on.

At National Bank of India our transfer-completed event drives the notification service. We started with Event Notification, but when the transfer service had a brief outage, the notification service could not fetch details and SMS messages were blocked, so we moved to Event-Carried State Transfer for the fields the notification and statement services needed — amount, beneficiary, account — and those consumers became autonomous and kept working during producer blips. We were careful not to slip into a fat event: we never put our internal ledger reference or risk bucket into the event, because that would have leaked internals and coupled those teams to our private model.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is this: Event Notification sends a tiny pointer and makes the consumer call back, trading payload size for runtime coupling and freshness, while Event-Carried State Transfer sends the data the consumer needs so it acts autonomously, trading a larger payload for resilience; I choose based on autonomy versus freshness and callback load, I use a versioned schema either way, and I never broadcast the whole aggregate as a god event.
